title: Chapter 211 – The Orchard of Hours
html:
[Terrace Five – Jian]

Jian pays the fare at first light.

He does it the way he has done everything on this road, which is to say slowly, with a clear head, and with the dull certainty that there is no version of the next few minutes in which he comes out ahead. The grain of salt lies in its iron bowl at the foot of the white stair. He picks it up between his thumb and forefinger. It is cold, and very small, and very bright, and it weighs exactly as much as a year.

```
ARK-7 // CROSSING
Fare, Terrace Four -> Terrace Five: 1 year of lifespan.
Lifespan: 92y 213d -> 91y 213d
Core: 82% (unchanged)
Note: The fare is taken from the PASSENGER, not the party.
Hua and Veyra Thann cross on their own accounts.
The Bridge is not used. Reason on file: time.
```

He reads the last line twice. He had not asked the machine to record a reason. It does that sometimes. It records what he has decided before he has finished deciding it, and he has never learned whether that is thoroughness or its own peculiar kind of loneliness.

He closes the grain in his fist.

Nothing happens. Then something in his chest gives a small, dry tick, like a watch that has lost a tooth, and he feels the year go. There is no pain. There is a sense of a door closing in a house he will never see again, in a room he has not yet visited. He opens his hand. The grain is gone. In the bowl, a thin line of white dust shows where it lay.

"That is the last of the easy ones," says the Cartographer, from the shadow of the shed.

Jian looks up.

The heavy man has walked out to the edge of the Terrace with his gray cloak over his arm. He has not slept, and it shows. But there is something different in his posture, a straightening of the shoulders that wasn't there yesterday, as though he has set down one of two heavy bags and discovered his back can still bear the other.

From Five on, the Cartographer says, the Road is not the same road.

"You told us there were Terraces and fares."

There are. But the Terraces above this one are not merely places. They are intervals. He rubs his eyes. Each one folds the hour. I do not know how else to say it. A day inside a Terrace is not a day outside. Ye Shuhan is nine days ahead of you, by the Sect's reckoning. By the Terrace's, he may be nine years.

Jian says nothing for a moment.

He had thought, in the dark hours of the night, that there might be something like this. He had read it in the Cartographer's maps, in the margins, where the heavy man drew a small curl beside the Fifth Terrace and wrote nothing at all. He had not wanted to ask.

"Which way does it run?"

Slower for you. Quicker for the world. The Cartographer lifts one shoulder. Or it is the other way about. I have never seen anyone come back to tell me.

---

It is Mo Yan he is dreading.

She is sitting in the dust at the end of the Quay, where she has sat for most of the night, with the white bell in her lap and the dead black one beside it. Veyra Thann has asked her to hold it, in the end. She said it quite simply, in the arch, in the quiet hour before midnight: I would like the child to keep her. She answers more easily to you. And Mo Yan, who has lost a name and gained a word, said yes.

Jian stops in front of her and crouches.

"I am not taking you up," he says.

"I know."

"It is not that I do not trust you. It is that I—"

"Don't." She doesn't look up. "I know what you're going to say. You're going to say it's too dangerous and I'm too small and someone has to stay with Lan Xiu."

"I was going to say the last of those."

"It's a good reason." She tilts the white bell in her lap. The line of light spills across her knee. "I'm not stupid, Jian. I know there's five of them still stone, and nobody else on this whole Terrace has paid. If I go, the Cartographer's all by himself with four hundred sleepers and he's old. And Sera—" She stops. Her chin trembles and she steadies it. "Sera talks to me."

He feels the floor tilt a little.

"She says things," Mo Yan says. "Not words. Not all the time. Just—a feeling. Like someone in the next bed saying are you awake? She keeps asking if I'm awake." She looks up at him at last, and her eyes are enormous in her small white face. "I think she's been alone for a very long time."

"She has."

"I can't leave her."

He wants to argue. He wants to say that a nine-year-old child has no business being the voice of a girl six hundred years dead in a place no living person understands. He wants to say that Veyra should have kept the bell. He wants to say a great many sensible things.

What he says is, "I will come back for you."

"I know."

"I give you my word."

"I know." She picks up the dead black bell, the Ferryman's, and presses it into his palm. The glass is cold as a coin. "Take this. It's empty. But it's the Ferryman's, and he said it has a girl in it, and I think she'd like to see the top."

Jian closes his fingers over the glass.

"I will carry her," he says.

Mo Yan nods. She stands up, and for a moment she is exactly the height of his ribs, a small, thin child in a stolen cloak, with a pale scar on her wrist where the mark has begun to fade. Then she steps forward and puts her arms around his waist and holds on, hard, the way you hold a rope.

He puts his good hand on her hair.

He does not say anything. There is nothing to say that she does not already know. They stand for a count of five, and then she lets go, and wipes her face on her sleeve, and goes to sit down beside Lan Xiu without looking back.

---

Veyra Thann is the last to cross.

She comes down the Quay slowly, in the thin blue light, with her hood drawn forward and her bandaged hand against her breastbone. She has taken the white bell's cloth from around her palm. Without the bell to fill it, the hand is a ruin: a flat, scarred hollow, ringed with ember, with a faint steady pulse in the base of the thumb.

She stops at the foot of the stair and looks up.

So, she says, in the cool blade-on-table voice. Five.

Jian waits.

I have not walked this stair in six hundred years, Veyra says. I walked it once, the other way, with my daughter's hand in mine. A pause. It was longer then.

"The Cartographer says it will fold the hour."

Yes. She sets her foot on the first step. He is right. Be prepared.

"For what?"

For the first time you look behind you, says Veyra Thann, and find that someone has moved the road.

She climbs.

Hua goes after her, with her hand tight on the mark and her mouth set in a line. Jian takes a last look at the Terrace behind him: the arch, the Quay, the shed with its lit stove, the line of blue-robed figures standing among the sleeping stone. Two small figures at the edge of the Quay, one tall in a blanket, one short in a cloak. A heavy man in gray, lifting a bandaged hand.

He lifts his own.

Then he turns his face to the mist and climbs.

---

The white stair is steeper than it looks. Jian counts the steps, because counting keeps his mind clear, and loses count at one hundred and nine. The mist is warm and smells of cut grass. Underfoot the stone is soft, almost springy, as though it has been trodden by a great many feet and has learned to give.

Somewhere around the hundred-and-fortieth step he realizes he can no longer hear the Terrace.

It isn't silence. The silence of Four was a living thing, a pressure. This is only absence, like the moment after a bell has stopped. He stops and listens. There is Hua's breathing, ahead of him. There is Veyra's step, light and exact. There is the rasp of his own breath, and the tick of his tremor against his sleeve. And beneath all of it, faint and steady, as if heard through a thick wall, a sound that he cannot name.

Ticking.

Not a clock. Something looser, more organic: the soft rapid ticking of a great many small things being counted. He tilts his head. It comes from above, from the mist, from the Fifth Terrace itself.

"Do you hear that?" Hua says.

It is the Orchard, says Veyra. Keep walking.

At the top of the stair there is a gate.

It is a plain wooden gate, hung between two pillars of rough white stone, and beyond it there is light. Not the pale dawn light of the Fourth Terrace but a warm, dense, golden light, like honey held up to a lamp. Jian's eyes water. He lifts his good hand to shade them.

Over the gate, carved into the lintel, there is a line of script in the Founders' hand.

```
ARK-7 // TRANSLATION (partial)
"HERE TIME IS GROWN, NOT SPENT."
Terrace Five: THE ORCHARD OF HOURS.
Keeper: unknown. Status: PRESENT.
Hazard flag: TEMPORAL. Cost model: UNKNOWN.
Rate of passage, Terrace vs. world: not yet measurable.
```

He closes the panel.

"Not yet measurable," he says under his breath.

It will be, Veyra answers.

She pushes open the gate.

---

The Orchard is a forest of small trees, in rows, in a vast bowl of golden grass.

They are not like any trees Jian has seen. They are no taller than a man, squat and twisted, with bark the color of old pewter and leaves like beaten brass. Every branch is heavy with fruit. The fruit is small, round, and clear, like a drop of amber, and inside each one something moves. It is slow. It is almost imperceptible. But he leans toward the nearest tree and sees it clearly: a tiny figure in each fruit, walking, tiny steps, in a tiny landscape of grass and stone.

"People," Hua whispers.

Not people. Veyra's voice has gone very quiet. Hours.

Hua draws a sharp breath. "That's—"

Each fruit is an hour of someone's life. They are grown here and ripen, and are gathered. The hooded head turns, slowly, taking in the rows. This is the Terrace's work. It is the engine of the Road. When a passenger pays a fare, the year goes into the soil, and the trees grow it into hours, and the hours go up to the top, to the Stair-Father's door, where they are used to hold the Seam.

Jian stares.

"You mean he is eating them."

I mean he is burning them. Like lamp oil. Her cool voice does not shake. It is a most economical system. The passengers pay, the trees grow, the Door burns. For six hundred years the Road has been a machine for turning the lifespans of the willing into a single steady flame. It is not a cruelty. It is a necessity. It was the Founders' only answer.

The tick of the trees fills the golden air. Jian sees now what he missed in the mist: the rows run on and on, farther than the eye can reach, and every tree is hung with hundreds of fruits, and every fruit holds a small bright life.

The two years he has paid are in here, somewhere.

He pushes the thought down.

"Who tends them?" he says.

That would be me, says a voice.

---

It comes from behind a tree, and it is not a voice at all but a rustling, dry and gentle, like a hand drawn across straw. A figure steps into the light between two rows of brass leaves. It is a woman, or something shaped like one, narrow and stooped, in a shapeless robe the color of dead grass. Her face is a mask of fine wrinkles, like a nut. Her eyes are a bright, leaf-dark green.

In her arms there is a basket of amber fruit.

She stops three paces away and looks at the three travelers one at a time. She takes her time. Then she says, in a voice like wind in a dry field:

"New growth. How lovely."

She sets down the basket.

"I am Sorrel," she says. "I am the Keeper of the Fifth Terrace, the Orchard of Hours. You have paid one year each, I think. No—" She tilts her head, and a rustle runs through her. "Not each. One year between you. Only the young man has paid. The old lady came on a coin older than the Road, and the girl on her mark."

"I came on my own account," says Hua.

"Of course you did." Sorrel smiles. It splits her walnut face in half. "Of course. Forgive an old woman. I have not had visitors in a long time, and everything goes to mush in the Orchard, eventually. Even the manners." She turns her bright green eyes on Veyra. "And you, my dear. You are the second key. Come down from sleep."

Sorrel, says Veyra Thann.

"Veyra." The wrinkled face softens. "You look terrible."

I am aware.

"You look wonderful, for a ghost." Sorrel steps forward, quickly, with the speed of a thing that has had a great deal of practice at appearing frail, and takes Veyra's bandaged hand in both of hers. "It is good to see you awake. It is good to see anyone awake. The trees have been so quiet."

You have not changed.

"I have changed a great deal," says the old woman tenderly. "I have become much more patient." She releases the hand and turns, briskly, to Jian. "And you. You are the one who carries the strange machine. Yes? I can hear it, you know. It is quite the loudest thing on the Road."

Jian goes cold.

He keeps his face still. "I do not know what you mean."

"Of course you don't." Sorrel bends and picks a single amber fruit from the basket, and holds it up between finger and thumb. The tiny figure inside is a man, in a gray robe, walking up a white stair. "Would you like to see?"

---

He doesn't want to.

He does. He wants to see more than he has wanted anything in weeks. It is the oldest craving of the body that is not his, the thirty years' hunger for an honest account of himself. But he has stood in front of enough Keepers by now to know that every offer is a cost, and he says, carefully:

"What would you ask for it?"

"Nothing," says Sorrel.

"Nothing."

"It's a gift, dear. I'm too old to haggle." She turns the fruit in the light. Inside it, the tiny gray man reaches the top of the stair and lifts his hand. "I only want you to look. And then I want you to tell me what you see."

Hua makes a small warning sound.

Veyra's voice, cool: Jian. Do not.

But Jian has already looked.

It is a very small thing. The fruit is the size of his thumbnail. The figure in it is the size of a grain of rice. But he knows the walk at once, the slight hitch in the left leg, the way the man's good hand finds his sleeve to hide the other. He knows the gray robe, the stoop, the careful way of holding the head.

It is himself.

He is looking at an hour of his own life. The hour he spent climbing the white stair, a few minutes ago. And around the tiny figure, drawn in the amber like the veins in a leaf, there are fine bright threads that run out of the fruit and into the air.

He follows them with his eyes. They go up, into the golden light. They go to the tree.

They go to every tree in the Orchard.

"There," says Sorrel gently. "Do you see? That's the thing about the strange machine. It's loud. It leaks. I can hear it from here, and so can the trees, and so can anything else that has ears." She lowers the fruit. "I'm so sorry, dear. Truly. It's the only way I could show you."

"Show me what?"

"That you've been leaving a trail," says the Keeper of the Orchard, "since the day you were born."

---

The panel comes. He had expected it to.

```
ARK-7 // ALERT
EXTERNAL EMISSION DETECTED.
Source: ARK-7 (self).
Signature: low-band, continuous, unshielded since activation.
Cause: Print unlock (Arc 6). Print draws on the Nine-Ring
as a template; the Ring leaks; ARK-7 leaks WITH it.
Receivers: UNKNOWN. At least one receiver is within range.
Location: Terrace Nine (inferred).
Recommended action: NONE AVAILABLE.
Silence of the emission would require unbuilding the Ring.
```

He reads it from top to bottom, and he understands.

It was the Print. All along. The Nine-Ring, the nine hosts, the nine days of life he had asked of his friends in order to mend one core, and the machine had said then that it leaked, and he had accepted it. He had thought the leak would only drain the Nine. He had not thought it would shout.

Every child it swallowed, he thinks. Every voice it borrowed. And all the time it was listening for the one that was loudest.

"Lin Jian," says Veyra Thann.

He raises his head.

"Whatever you read just now," she says, "you will tell us later. The Keeper has done you a service. You know now what we are climbing toward. A thing that has been listening for you since the day you used the Print." Her voice is flat and calm, and Hua has gone white beside her. "It does not change the road. It changes only the pace."

"How?"

"Ask her."

Sorrel is smiling.

"We have eleven days," says the Keeper of the Orchard. "If you run. Twenty, if you walk. Beyond that, the Door will notice, and then it will not matter what you carry." She lays the amber fruit gently on the top of the basket. "In the Orchard, an hour is a thing you grow. You may have as many as you like. But the world will not wait for you, dears. It never has."

---

Sorrel walks them down the Ripening Row.

She does it at a stately pace, with her basket on her arm, and she talks the whole way, in the gentle rustling voice of a woman who has not had an audience in centuries and is determined not to waste one. The golden grass whispers about their ankles. The twisted trees tick and tick. Hua walks close to Jian's shoulder, her mark-hand curled against her chest, and Veyra follows a pace behind, silent as a shadow.

"You have all read the rule," Sorrel says. "Here time is grown, not spent. Most do not understand it until they have stood here a day. I will make it plain, because I am fond of you, and because I am very bored."

She stops at a tree that is a little taller than the others, with a curved trunk and a bench of white stone at its foot.

"A cultivator on the Road of Nine," she says, "must reach the Nascent Soul before the Ninth Door. This is not a rule of the Founders. It is merely arithmetic. A man below the Nascent Soul cannot survive the light at the top, and a man above it need not fear the Seam. So the Road has a means of getting you there." She pats the bench. "Sit."

Jian does not sit.

"Go on," Sorrel says, with a smile. "It will not bite. It will only grow."

He looks at Veyra. The hood gives him nothing. He looks at Hua. She gives a small, strained nod.

He sits.

The bench is cool, and the tree above it leans in as though listening. Sorrel takes an amber fruit from the branch, a fruit with nothing in it but light, and holds it out.

"This is an empty hour," she says. "Nothing in it yet. You eat it, and you sit, and you cultivate. For every hour you sit, the tree grows a day around you. For every day, a season. Ten years of work in a month, a hundred in a year, if you have the patience. Your core will deepen, your meridians will harden, your Nascent Soul will form in the quiet of the fruit. And all the while—" she lifts one finger "—the world outside does not rest."

"The world outside moves faster."

"Eighty times faster, at the Seventh. Forty, here." Sorrel's green eyes are kind. "A month in the Orchard is three years in the Mortal Realm. A year is forty. You see the difficulty."

Jian sees it.

He sees, all at once, the Wall and the tower and the man bound to the tower. He sees Qinghe, cooking by sound, and Kuang planning a funeral for a roll of two thousand names. He sees a small girl in a nursery with a Lin blood fault, lent two percent by a child who was already tired. He sees them age.

He sees all of them age, while he sits on a stone bench and grows.

"The Nascent Soul takes eighty years," he says slowly. "By the Lin reckoning. I told the Council it would."

"At the Seventh Terrace you could do it in a year," says Sorrel. "Perhaps two. If you do not dally."

"And outside?"

"Eighty years," the Keeper agrees comfortably, "give or take."

The golden light is very bright. Jian realizes he has stopped hearing the trees.

"There is another way," Veyra says quietly. "It is called the Bridge."

"It is," says Sorrel.

"It carries no time with it. It crosses the Terraces in a single stride. It would put Lin Jian at the Ninth Door in four days. At Core, with his core at eighty-two percent."

"At the Ninth Door," Sorrel agrees, "in the light. And you know what the light does to a Core."

"Yes," says Veyra Thann. "I held a Core there once."

She says nothing more. She does not have to.

Jian looks at the empty amber fruit in the old woman's palm. He looks at his shaking hand, and the faint line of the tremor, and the places on the skin where the Print's mending has left a pale web of scar. He thinks of the oldest rule he owns: every advantage has a named cost. And he thinks, with a clarity that is almost calm, that the cost has finally been named.

Eighty years of his friends' lives, against four days of his own.

He stands up from the bench.

"Not yet," he says.

Sorrel's wrinkled face does not change. "Of course," she says. "Take your time. In the Orchard, you have as much as you can bear."

---

Jian turns, slowly, and looks back.

He had meant only to check the gate. He had meant only to confirm what he already knew: the white stair, the mist, the Fourth Terrace somewhere beneath them, and two small figures at the edge of the Quay.

The gate stands open. Beyond it there is gold and brass and the tick of ten thousand tiny hours.

There is no stair.

There is no mist. There is no Quay, no shed, no Cartographer, no child in a stolen cloak. There is only a wall of warm golden light, and in the middle of it, drawn faintly on the air like a thumbprint on glass, the shape of a small hand, pressed flat, as though somebody on the far side had reached up to touch it.

I did tell you, says Veyra Thann, very gently, from behind him, about the moving of the road.

Jian does not answer. He stands with the Ferryman's dead black bell in his fist and his ruined hand shaking in his sleeve, and he watches the small pale print fade from the light until there is nothing there at all.
